shortTitle: Q.2941 GIT and UUS for IP
summary: Assigns values for the information field and protocol identifier used in ATM Q.2941 Generic Identifier and Q.2957 user-to-user signaling when carrying Internet protocols. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This is a small lookup table that says which code number means Internet traffic in an old phone-style network signaling system.

questions: what is the q.2941 generic identifier
how does rsvp run over atm signaling
what is the ipv4 session identifier in atm
subtitle: Code points that let ATM signaling carry IP session identifiers and RSVP messages.

tldr.problem: To set up an ATM virtual circuit for an Internet session, the signaling must carry an identifier for that session, or even the setup protocol itself, but no values were assigned for Internet protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns values in the Q.2941 Generic Identifier (session identifiers for IPv4 and IPv6, an MPLS VCID) and in the Q.2957 User-user information element (protocol identifier 0x06, with RSVP messages as one payload).
tldr.outcome: It supplies the framework for long-lived and QoS-sensitive sessions over ATM, but only the assignments. The full interoperable protocol is left to a separate document.

today: RFC 3033 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says it assigns fields only and leaves the complete interoperable protocol to a separate document.

sections.title: Purpose of the Document
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how the information field and protocol identifier are assigned in two ITU-T signaling elements, the Q.2941 Generic Identifier and the Q.2957 User-to-user Signaling, when they are used for the Internet protocol. It is designed for advanced B-ISDN signaling support, especially for a connection that corresponds to a session in the Internet protocol.

It calls the specification an indispensable framework for implementing long-lived and QoS-sensitive session transfers over ATM. It also says plainly what it is not: it assigns fields and identifiers only, and may not specify a complete protocol for interoperable implementation, because that is beyond its scope and will be specified in a separate document.
sections.eli5: Two systems need a shared dictionary so they know that a certain code means Internet traffic. This document writes down that dictionary and nothing more.

sections.title: Session-Related ATM Connections
sections.content:
The motivation is multimedia. Voice, audio and video applications want QoS-guaranteed communication, which the best-effort IP network does not give. The RFC points to the B-ISDN features of high speed, logical multiplexing with VP/VC, and flexible QoS management per VC as a natural fit.

Long-lived sessions. A new session is first forwarded over a default VC between the routers. If a router detects that it is long-lived, it sets up a new VC and moves the session onto it. The called router's signaling entity must recognize that the call belongs to an Internet session and tell the IP layer, so the signaling needs a session identifier. Of the information elements that could carry it (B-LLI, B-HLI, User-user and Generic Identifier), the RFC picks the Generic Identifier as the most appropriate.

QoS-sensitive sessions. Here the call setup is started explicitly by a setup protocol such as RSVP. The RFC describes two schemes: send the setup protocol over a default or particular VC, so the session and VC are established one after the other, or carry it as an information element in the B-ISDN signaling, so both are established together. The second is easier to implement, since admission control and watchdog timer handling are simpler, and lets a negotiated QoS shape the VC. It cannot support a case where a PVC carries the session, so both procedures need to be considered. The second scheme needs a User-user information element large enough to carry the setup protocol.
sections.eli5: When a phone-call-like link is opened for a long video chat, the network needs a way to say which chat the link is for. Sometimes it also needs to carry the request for special treatment along with the call.

sections.title: The Two Signaling Elements
sections.content:
The Generic Identifier carries identifiers between end users. It is an optional information element for Q.2931 and Q.2971 UNI signaling, and a message such as SETUP, CONNECT or ADD PARTY may contain up to three of them. Its maximum length is 63 octets. The network may check its contents. The element starts with identifier 0x7F, then fields for the related standard or application, and then one or more identifiers, each made of a type, a length and a value.

The User-to-user Signaling carries user data instead, through the User-user information element (identifier 0x7E). It has a protocol discriminator that names the upper-layer protocol, followed by the user information. Its maximum length is 133 octets. The network does not check its contents, and it can interwork with the user-user element in Q.931 N-ISDN signaling, which the Generic Identifier cannot.

The RFC notes the two look similar but follow different exception-handling rules, because the Generic Identifier moves identifiers between c-planes while the User-to-user Signaling moves user data.
sections.eli5: One element is like a name tag attached to the call. The other is like a sealed note that the network passes along without reading.

sections.title: Generic Identifier Assignments
sections.content:
For the Identifier related standard/application field, the RFC assigns 0x03 to IPv4, 0x04 to ST2+, 0x05 to IPv6 and 0x06 to MPLS. For the Identifier type field it assigns 0x01 for Session and 0x02 for Resource, reserves 0x10 to 0xFD for IANA assignment, and uses 0xFE for Experiment/Organization specific.

Three identifiers are defined. The IPv4 session identifier (type Session, length 13 octets) holds, in order, the source address, destination address, protocol, source port and destination port. The IPv6 session identifier is the same shape with 16-octet addresses and a length of 37 octets. The MPLS VCID (type Resource, length 4 octets) holds a VCID as defined in RFC 3038. The Experiment/Organization identifier begins with a 3-octet organizationally unique identifier (OUI).

The session identifiers are meant for explicit reservations only. If wild-card associations are needed later, another identifier type will be used.

The document does not specify the order of multiple identifiers, or what it means when identifiers of the same type repeat or an element holds none. When a calling party sends SETUP or ADD PARTY with up to three Generic Identifier elements, the CONNECT or ADD PARTY ACK returned must contain at least one, though it need not repeat the same identifiers. That allows identifier negotiation, whose detailed procedure is not specified. A network that does not support the element clears the call, discards the element, or discards the message.
sections.eli5: A session identifier is like writing both addresses and both door numbers of a conversation on the label, so everyone knows exactly which conversation the link is for.

sections.title: User-User Information Element Assignments
sections.content:
For Internet use, the protocol discriminator is 0x06 (Internet protocol/application). The first octet of the user information is then the Internet protocol/application identifier: 0x00 is reserved, 0x01 is reserved for ST2+, 0x02 is an RSVP message, 0x03 to 0xFD is reserved for IANA assignment, 0xFE is Experiment/Organization specific and 0xFF is reserved.

For an RSVP message, the rest of the field holds the message. The RFC says the SETUP message may contain the RSVP Resv message, CONNECT may contain ResvConf, and RELEASE may contain ResvErr or ResvTear. The Experiment/Organization form starts with a 3-octet OUI.

As with the Generic Identifier, a SETUP or ADD PARTY carrying a User-user element must be answered by a CONNECT or ADD PARTY ACK that also contains one, though not necessarily with the same content. A network lacking support clears the call or discards the element or message.

An appendix, which the RFC says is not part of the standard, gives matching assignments for ST2+: a session identifier carrying a 6-octet Stream ID, and ST2+ SCMP messages (identifier 0x01).
sections.eli5: The sealed note starts with a code saying what kind of note it is. One code means a reservation request, and some codes are held back for later.

sections.title: IANA Considerations and Open Issues
sections.content:
Two ranges are reserved for IANA. Identifier type values 0x10 to 0xFD in the Generic Identifier (when the related standard is IPv4, ST2+, IPv6 or MPLS), and identifier values 0x03 to 0xFD in the User-user element (when the protocol discriminator is Internet protocol/application). Both are allocated through an IETF Consensus action, following RFC 2434.

The RFC lists two open issues. One is Generic Identifier support for session aggregation, which may be needed in a backbone, where a wild-card aggregated identifier might be feasible but the aggregation model in ATM VCs should be clarified first. The other is support for the IPv6 flow label and traffic classes, whose semantics were not clear at the time.
sections.eli5: Some code numbers are held back in a drawer. A new one can be taken out only after the community agrees.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the assignments do not weaken the security of B-ISDN signaling. It adds one suggestion: if an incoming SETUP message contains the calling party number, and that number was verified and passed by the ATM network or provided by the network, it is feasible to use it for part of the calling party authentication.
sections.eli5: Adding a label to the call does not make it less safe. If the network vouches for who is calling, that can help check the caller.

items.label: RSVP message
items.desc: The rest of the field holds an RSVP message.
